provenance: Anon. sale, Sotheby's, London, 3 October 2007, lot 59. | Private collection, USA (acquired from the above sale). | | This elegant three-quarter length portrait shows an unidentified woman dressed fashionably and in a style that suggests a date for the painting of sometime in the 1880s. Carlo (later anglicised to Charles) Perugini was born in Naples in 1839. He met Leighton in Rome in the early 1850s, and may have served as a model for the painting Cimabue's Madonna (Royal Collection), upon which Leighton was then working. In the later 1850s, Perugini trained under Ary Scheffer in Paris. He then transferred to London in 1863, commencing as an exhibitor at the Royal Academy that same year. | | Perugini's style of painting, which is softly naturalistic and fluently handled, and in which is found a particular feeling for the textures of skin and cloth, owes much to the example of Leighton. Like his mentor, Perugini succeeds in making his compositions harmonious and elegantly unified, and introduces a living quality to what he paints by their freshness of texture and glowing animation. In the present work Perugini shows himself adept at the representation of landscape, with a lovely distant view of sea and coast forming the background to the portrait. The artist would certainly have known Leighton's own landscape sketches, with their remarkable feeling for the quality and direction of light. Here, the impressionistic freshness of the natural setting makes a delightful contrast to the elegance and sophistication of the model, as evidenced by the elaborate style of her dress and the composure of her demeanour. | | Perugini's portraits of young women are often supposed to represent his wife Kate, the daughter of Charles Dickens who was also a painter. She had previously been married to the artist Charles Allston Collins but had been widowed in 1873. It may be suggested that the work was commissioned as a marriage portrait. The model wears a rosebud at her bosom, which may be seen as a symbol of her youthful and unfolding beauty, while her wedding-ring is visible on her left hand. The connection with Dickens is possibly referred to by the open book the sitter is holding in her right hand. | | We are grateful to Christopher Newall for composing this catalogue entry.

artwork_title: Portrait of Frederick Richards Leyland, bust-length
material: coloured chalks on pale blue paper
provenance: Commissioned by the sitter as a wedding present for his eldest daughter on her marriage to Stevenson Hamilton in 1879. | By descent to Squadron-Leader D.L. Stevenson. | Anon. sale, Christie's, London, 9 November 1971, lot 150. | With The Fine Art Society, London, 1973. | Private collection, UK. | | Literature | Virginia Surtees, Dante Gabriel Rossetti: A Catalogue Raisonné, London, 1971, vol. Bancroft, Jr., and Related Pre-Raphaelite Collections (in the Delaware Art Museum), Wilmington, 1978, p. 130. | | The present lot is a portrait of the Liverpool shipowner and art collector Frederick Richards Leyland (1831-1892). It was commissioned by Leyland to give to his daughter Frances (known as Fanny) on the occasion of her marriage to Hamilton Stevenson, the son of the Newcastle-upon-Tyne-based industrialist and collector Alexander Stevenson (1826-1900). | | Leyland was a handsome man and with a very distinctive physiognomy, being described in Clement Jones's 1934 history of ship-owning as one who 'with his fine head and pointed beard, had the appearance of a Spanish Grandee adventurer; and [the description continued] he had the coolness and effrontery to match. His passage through life was mainly in the teeth of a storm.'1 Rossetti's portrait shows Leyland, head and shoulders, facing slightly to the left. He is wearing a dark coat and with the style of frilled shirt that he habitually wore. | | Rossetti described his progress on Leyland's portrait in a letter to Frederick Shields of 16 July 1879: 'I am doing a head of him for a wedding present to his eldest daughter, but have begun two already without quite pleasing myself. His head is really fine, but there are difficult points in it.'2 The earlier attempts to capture his appearance referred to in the letter to Shields are untraced. Rossetti's chalk drawing of Leyland in oval format (Bancroft Collection, Delaware Art Museum, Wilmington; Surtees catalogue number 346), although said also to date from 1879, must in fact have originated from several years earlier, as the sitter has there the appearance of a younger man – with dark bushy beard and longer flowing hair than is seen in the present drawing. Four days after writing to Shields, Rossetti reported the completion of the present drawing in a letter to Theodore Watts-Dunton: 'I've given Leyland a frill and everything & he's All There now.'3 Rossetti explained the sad conclusion to the matter in a letter to Jane Morris of 4th of March of the following year: following their wedding in July 1879 the Stevensons had set out for Italy, being joined there by Alexander Stevenson and his two other daughters. However, and while still in Italy, Frances Stevenson died in childbirth just eight months after her marriage. Rossetti concluded: 'I made for her a drawing of her father as a wedding present. This (through framing delays) was never sent to Scotland till she had gone to Italy, & now she is dead!'4 | | Even despite the tragic circumstances of the present drawing, the work makes an important and fascinating link between two of the most remarkable British collector-patrons of the second half of the nineteenth century. F.R. Leyland had been brought up in circumstances of extreme poverty and had commenced his working life as an errand boy for the Liverpool ship-owner John Bibby. Nonetheless, by hard graft and ruthless business practices, he eventually came to own a fleet of more than twenty ships, operating between Liverpool, Boston, and ports of the Mediterranean. Leyland lived in an Elizabethan country house called Speke Hall near Liverpool, and in a vast mansion in Prince's Gate in Kensington, which was rebuilt for him by Richard Norman Shaw. In these two houses he assembled collections of Old Master paintings, and which were hung in combination with superb works by Burne-Jones, Albert Moore, Leighton, Ford Madox Brown and James Whistler, displayed together with precious works of art and in astonishing aesthetic style interiors (most notably the 'Peacock Room', designed by Whistler). Leyland's acquisition of a group of about eighteen paintings by Rossetti had commenced in 1867 with the purchase of Monna Rosa, a portrait of Leyland's wife Frances (Surtees 198). Alexander Stevenson was Glaswegian by birth but was established on Tyneside by the mid-1840s. His wealth seems to have derived principally from the various chemical works for which he worked, notably the Jarrow Chemical Company of which he was a senior partner, as well as from shipbroking. He and his wife Alice lived in Tynemouth but also had an estate in Argyllshire and a house in Surrey. Stevenson possessed a number of works by Rossetti, including autograph replicas of The Loving Cup (Surtees 201 R.3) and Lady Lilith (Surtees 205 R.2), of each of which subject Leyland had the prime version. In addition, and as described by F.G. Stephens in his article 'The Private Collections of England – Tynemouth – Gateshead' the collection included a large group of drawings by Simeon Solomon and a painting by Albert Moore.5 | | 1 Quoted in Stephen Wildman, Waking Dreams – The Art of the Pre-Raphaelites from the Delaware Art Museum, Alexandria, 2004, p. 204. | 2 William E. Fredeman (ed.), The Correspondence of Dante Gabriel Rossetti, volume 8, Woodbridge, 2009, p. 302. | 3 Fredeman, op. cit., volume 8, 2009, p. 306. | 4 Fredeman, op. cit., volume 9, 2010, p. 78. | 5 Athenaeum, 27 September 1873, pp. 406-9. | | We are grateful to Christopher Newall for composing this catalogue entry.

He himself was a man of intense Christian faith, and the work in question is one of a group of religious paintings which are amongst his most personal and greatest achievements. | | The subject of The Good Shepherd | In Dyce's painting the robed figure of a shepherd leads a flock of sheep through an open gateway into a sunlit pasture. An ivy-clad fence runs away into the landscape, with a mountainous horizon. A tree stands beside the fence, with bare branches and a contorted stem, while in the far distance on the left stand further trees before a group of farm buildings. The ground across which the barefooted figure walks is stony, but the pasture into which he and his accompanying sheep enter offers the sustenance of fresh grass and water. The shepherd holds in his right hand a crook and looks downwards at the lamb which he holds in his left arm with clear awareness of the solemn duty of caring for his flock. | | When the painting was shown at the Royal Academy in the summer of 1859, and then again at the Liverpool Academy later in the same year, verse 11, Chapter 40, of the Book of Isaiah was attached in an abbreviated form: 'He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.' This text forms the opening of what is known as the 'Deutero-Isaiah', the oldest part of the Book of Isaiah and which was written by an anonymous author in the 6th century BCE at the time of the Babylonian exile. It describes how God determined to protect Jerusalem and that it was his intention to send a messiah to allow the Jewish people safe return to their city. The text pleads for the protection of the poor and dispossessed, but claims that righteousness comes not from Israel's Covenant with God but from God's essential holiness. | | In Dyce's painting, the sheepfold stands for the Promised Land; the sheep for the people of Israel and the shepherd for their Messiah. The Messiah is in turn a type of Jesus Christ, the Saviour. The painting is an exploration of typological symbolism – the parallels between events described in the Old and New Testaments and the links between types and antitypes – and of which study Victorian scholars were so preoccupied. In The Good Shepherd, Dyce created a universal symbol of loving care – which stands for the figure of Christ and of the Christian virtues. | | Images of the Good Shepherd as a type of Christ occur frequently in early Christian art, for example in wall paintings in the Roman catacombs, in sculpted sarcophagi, and in mosaics (as for example in the sixth-century Mausoleum of Galle Placidia in Ravenna), from a time before the conventions by which Christ was to be represented were established. Therefore, while on other occasions Dyce treated the figure of Christ following Biblical narrative, with The Good Shepherd he offered an image of a man like any other, performing a mundane duty, but who stands for the antitype of Christ and exemplifies his teaching. The work is therefore both absolutely immediate and direct in its message, treated as it is with scrupulous honesty and care, but also a highly sophisticated meditation on a particular type of Christian imagery. | | The precise date and likely setting of The Good Shepherd. | Although first exhibited in 1859, The Good Shepherd appears to have been painted two years earlier. In 1856 a cartoon or preparatory drawing apparently related to the same composition was shown amongst the drawings and miniatures at the Royal Academy summer exhibition (as mentioned by James Dafforne in his Art Journal article describing Dyce's work), while further evidence supporting a date of 1857 for the present painting is provided by the reference to it in a letter dated 10 September 1857 in which the painter listed his recent works: 'Here is my account of dispatch of business for the first part of this year [...] painted a picture of the Good Shepherd'. It seems likely that the physical setting of the subject was inspired by places Dyce had visited on the Isle of Arran on the west coast of Scotland, to which place he is known to have gone in or before 1856, or in Dumfriesshire and Galloway, where he had family friends who he was known on occasions to visit. The close observation of detail, as in for example, the circular feeding byre around the trunk of the dead tree at the upper left-hand corner of the composition, leaves no doubt but that this was an actual place. In the 1850s Dyce was committed to the principle of working out of doors so as to gain authentic representation of landscape and natural detail, as Jennifer Melville observed in 2006: 'Dyce imbues his paintings with an intensity of vision that come through direct observation of nature. He combines this with a spirituality that comes from his own deeply felt faith. This gives each work a personal dimension that is unique.' | | British artists working in the middle years of the nineteenth century occasionally provided landscape settings for their Old and New Testament subjects which were intended to represent or at least to suggest the topography of the Holy Land, whether treated from the imagination or on the basis of actual exploration and study. Alternatively, and as on this occasion, painters were content to represent Biblical subjects in landscape settings with which they themselves were immediately familiar. Debate about the appropriateness of Biblical subjects in settings other than those of a supposed Holy Land recurred. Of Dyce's subject The Man of Sorrows (National Gallery of Scotland, Edinburgh), which shows Christ seated on a glacially smoothed rock in a wider upland setting which probably represents Aberdeenshire, F.G. Stephens, writing in the Athenaeum, asked why the artist had not made a similar attempt: 'But why – with all this literalness – not be completely loyal, and paint Christ himself in the land where he really lived?' In fact, as Michaela Giebelhausen has observed, 'Stephens either failed to realise, or simply ignored, the fact that the jarring juxtaposition between figure and landscape [in The Man of Sorrows but the same response might apply to The Good Shepherd] was intentional and essential to the meaning of the painting [...] In the face of the doubt and anxiety characteristic of the age, Dyce offered an incongruous image of Christ and invited his viewer to make a leap of faith which demanded the acceptance of Christ's divinity notwithstanding such questioning.' In his later paintings of religious themes Dyce had no need for such motifs to lend authenticity to his religious subjects, so that The Good Shepherd (described by Marcia Pointon as 'aggressively contemporary') is striking for its verisimilitude and authenticity. | | The sincerity of Christian message radiates from every element of the composition and requires no elucidation while it is the actuality of the scene as a real place that is so compelling. Even the physiognomy of the figure of the shepherd and his beard and hair, which seems to have a reddish tinge, allows the spectator to feel himself in the presence of one who is recognisably Scottish rather than Semitic. Pointon elaborated on the painter's need to represent a religious subject as something entirely real: 'Dyce, as an extremely active and articulate High Churchman, believed in a contemporary Christ. His deliberate presentation of biblical characters as very human and existing in a physical environment described in concrete detail is essential to his theological interpretation of his subject and is not merely a means of evoking the ethos of an earlier style of art or of creating an anachronistic appeal.' | | Dyce and the Pre-Raphaelites | The point of intersection between Dyce and the Pre-Raphaelites (they themselves were approximately a generation younger than he) was in the creation of religious subjects which would inform, educate and instil faith. To paint carefully and according to the principle of 'truth to nature' was for him, as it was for William Holman Hunt, a way of honouring God, for he believed that – although the physical world might be explained in scientific terms – nonetheless the universe was a divine creation. In 1850 Dyce persuaded John Ruskin to look carefully at John Everett Millais's painting Christ in the House of his Parents (Tate), shown that year at the Royal Academy, and with the consequence that the critic took up the cause of Pre-Raphaelitism | with letters to The Times and the pamphlet Pre-Raphaelitism. Dyce visited Italy three times, and in fact had a larger knowledge of European art – and particularly early Italian schools of painting – than any member of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. The interdependence of Dyce and the Pre-Raphaelites is partial but mutually important; as Allen Staley wrote of him: 'His work is not central to the movement, but with sobriety and discipline he built upon Pre-Raphaelitism to paint a handful of the most memorable pictures of the Victorian era.' | | Dyce the Christian polymath | Dyce was a man engaged with a multitude of different interests – spiritual and scientific – and in addition to his commitments as a painter and public servant. In all respects, he believed in the power of art to convey the Christian message. In 1839, he had been a founder member of the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge (an organisation led by members of the Tractarian movement, the purpose of which was to return the Anglican Church to its pre-Reformation function to inspire Christian belief). In the early days of the Society there was discussion about how a projected book paraphrasing the Gospels of the New Testament should be illustrated, either with engravings after Old Masters, or – as advocated by Dyce – with images made by contemporary artists which he believed would be more clearly understood by a modern audience. In 1856, in a letter in which he reflected upon how churches might be decorated to encourage faith, he commented on the sixteenth-century text known as the 'King's Book' (1543), in which as he explained 'not only justifies but orders the erection of images of Christ [...] it also directs all curates to instruct their parishioners in the lessons taught by such images and pictures.' | | Ruskin and Dyce knew each other without ever becoming friends. At least twice they clashed openly, once in a dispute about how art should be taught (as explained by Lindsay Errington in her 1992 article 'Ascetics and sensualists, William Dyce's views on Christian art'), but before that when Dyce issued a contradiction of opinions expressed by Ruskin in his text Notes on the Construction of Sheepfolds (1851). In the early 1850s Ruskin was an Evangelical Protestant, virulently opposed to the extension of Roman Catholic influence in Britain at a time of the establishment of a Catholic church hierarchy. Dyce, by contrast, was a High Church Episcopalian Anglo-Catholic, and one who occasionally contemplated conversion (following the lead, as it would have been, of his friend John Henry Newman). Thus, Ruskin and Dyce differed on the principles of organisation, function and purpose of the Church. Ruskin's Notes on the Construction of Sheepfolds was intended as a supplement to his three-volume Stones of Venice, the sub-text of which was that the true expression of faith depended upon a personal freedom which might never be achieved by people living under the authority of the Roman Church. Dyce's response was to defend the role of the priesthood, trusting the church administration with responsibility to care for the people and their needs. As Emily Hope Thomson has explained, Dyce was the first to make 'a written and later a pictorial response' to Ruskin's text. The written response took the form of Notes on Shepherds and Sheep: A Letter to John Ruskin (1851); the pictorial response was The Good Shepherd. The argument between the two men hinged on whether the person of faith might believe that they were in direct communication with Christ, or whether it was accepted that an appointed priesthood might stand proxy for the Saviour. | | How The Good Shepherd was received | The Good Shepherd was met with huge enthusiasm when first seen in public in 1859. The Art Journal, in its review of the Royal Academy exhibition said of it: 'This is a literal presentation of the Saviour as the Shepherd; he gathers the sheep into the fold, bearing in his arms a lamb, and being followed by the sheep as he enters. [...] It is painted in the most perfect purity of feeling; it is, in truth, a work of the highest order, compelling not only reverence for the theme, but respect for the artist who could so well conceive, and so admirably picture it.' A year later, James Dafforne, in his Art Journal article describing Dyce's work, wrote: 'Neither have we forgotten "The Good Shepherd," exhibited in 1859 [...] The title sufficiently indicates the subject, which has been literally carried out, in a spirit and with a feeling that, viewed either artistically or devotionally, leaves nothing to be desired: it is altogether a work of the highest character.' In the bedroom of an ancient country house, a beautiful young woman kneels in a prayerful attitude beside a large brass-studded leather trunk, her arms resting on it as, lost in thoughts of her absent love, she gazes towards the light that filters through the casement window. Only two small panes are visible but these are sufficient to suggest that it is a frosty moonlit night. Inside, all is dark and shrouded. Her narrow bed stands against the wall, its frame adorned with Gothic finials. In the letter quoted above, Hughes' own itemising of the accessories underlines the importance he attached to them, and the results are patent. The solid painting, the meticulous attention to detail, and the lighting effects make this one of Hughes's most successful single figure compositions. | | The picture has been described as echoing Hughes' Pre-Raphaelite past1, and although the lighting and colour are more brilliant, in subject, composition and mood it is indeed reminiscent of examples like Millais' Mariana (1851, Tate Gallery). Carbonell. | | Tangier had long been a draw for European Orientalists, among the first visitors being Eugène Delacroix, John Frederick Lewis and David Roberts in the 1830s. Later visitors included Alfred Dehodencq and Mariano Fortuny, the latter's work 'helping to construct the myth of Oriental Tangier' according to Jordi Carbonell1. Benjamin-Constant first visited Tangier in 1870 then returned, at the behest of Charles Tissot, a friend of his father, in 1871, spending 18 months working in the city. As George Clairin, who met Benjamin- Constant during his first visit, later noted, 'his entire oeuvre was subjected to the fortunate and beneficial influence of Tangier; his entire Orient was Morocco ... he always carried with him this first impression of Tangier, white and bright.'2 | | During his sojourn in the early 1870s, Benjamin-Constant made numerous sketches of the city and its inhabitants, working them up into compositions back in his studio, with the many Islamic objects and artifacts he collected used as props. These would inform his output for the next ten years. | | Benjamin-Constant's meticulous attention to architectural and costume detail reflects both his fascination with the visual richness of Tangier and the broader European interest for the exotic. His use of vibrant colour, dramatic lighting, and carefully orchestrated figures conveys a sense of theatricality, while maintaining ethnographic precision in the depiction of dress, weaponry, and domestic objects. This combination of accuracy and artistic flourish helped solidify his reputation as a leading Orientalist painter of his generation. He was one of the founding members of the Société des Peintres Orientalistes Français in 1893, alongside artists such as Alphonse-Étienne Dinet. | | Compositionally, the present lot calls to mind The Pasha's Soldiers (circa 1880, Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design), with soldiers at rest among the ramparts of the 'White City', the sparkling Mediterranean sea beyond. By presenting soldiers at rest, rather than in action, he captures a moment of calm and humanizes the figures, allowing viewers to engage with them on both a formal and narrative levels. Such compositional choices were influential among his contemporaries and contributed to the enduring appeal of his Moroccan subjects in European collections. | | Henry James Turner (1831-1924), who owned the present lot in the early 20th Century, was a successful industrialist, who assembled a large collection of art by contemporary British and continental artists. provenance: Private collection, UK. | | Of all the animals that John Frederick Lewis painted, the camel was the most frequently depicted. His fascination is revealed by the sheer number of sketches and finished paintings, both in oil and watercolour. He would paint them in detail obsessively, as noted by Ruskin, who asserted that 'Let him examine, for instance, with a good lens, the eyes of the camels, and he will find that there is as much painting beneath their drooping fringes as would, with most painters, be thought enough for the whole head'.1 | | Lewis used his noted realism, his unmatched skill in drawing and painting textiles, by studying the elaborate trappings of camel saddles, with their flamboyant tassels and subtly woven saddle cloths. He understood the pride that camel owners took in making the best of their favourite animals. Consequently, there are a significant number of his studies and sketches of these dromedaries now in museums, art galleries and private collections throughout the world. | | In the early 1870s, Lewis decided to finish some early sketches and paintings which were still in his studio, perhaps to make preparations in order to provide the maximum value for his wife Marian when she finally inherited his estate. He engaged a studio assistant to help him with this task. This seems to be what happened to the present sketch. | | Briony Llewellyn discovered that Lewis had at least one studio assistant, called William Britten (1848-1916) a late Pre-Raphaelite painter. He helped Lewis with some pictures in the early 1870s when Lewis was in obvious physical decline. The painter Frederick Goodall is also said to have helped Lewis, working with him on a version of The Dellal (1875). Lewis had obviously influenced Goodall in his earlier years, and probably inspired the younger artist in his own accurate depictions of the camel. | | The central part of the present lot is most likely an early study for the painting called On the banks of the Nile, Upper Egypt (1876, now in the collection of the Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Collection) although there are other paintings dating back to the late 1840s that are candidates as well. It is probable that it was Britten who put in the background of the pyramid of Giza, as an obvious way of localizing it. Incidentally, the painting at Yale also has the work of a studio assistant in the background, in particular, the images of the women on the left. Lewis, in his response concerning this picture describes the techniques, the pigments and the support he used. He also states that the painting was 'sketched out about ten years ago – put aside until 1872. Touched on occasionally until 1875. Scarcely considered as finished yet'.2 | | The present sketch is a well-documented work that combines two phases of Lewis's work and is one of the few left that are not in museums and art galleries worldwide. | | We are grateful to Charles Newton for his assistance in cataloguing this lot. The work will be included in the forthcoming catalogue raisonné of the artist's work. | | 1Academy Notes, 1856, p. 74. | 2Royal Academy of Arts, Members' methods of procedure ('Leighton's Painting Process'), 1876, RAA/LIB/4/1.

provenance: Anon. sale, Maitre Blache, Paris, 3 June 1981. | Private collection, UK. | | A founder of the Society for French Orientalist Painters, Alphonse-Étienne Dinet's love of North Africa and its people was so strong that he eventually converted to Islam in 1905, taking the name Nasrédine. His knowledge of the Arabic language allowed him access to remote locations and enabled him to capture a more intimate portrayal of the life of North Africa. | | Few Orientalist artists are remembered as national icons in the countries they depicted. Yet Dinet (1861-1929), a French-born and Paris-trained painter secured the posthumous reputation of 'master' in Algeria where he lived and worked for almost fifty years. The son of a prosperous lawyer, Dinet first completed his military service in Normandy before enrolling in the École des Beaux-Arts and the Galland atelier where he studied painting and anatomy, eventually moving onto the Académie Julian for the remainder of his education. His paintings received critical acclaim at the Salon des Artistes Français and afterward, in 1884, Dinet embarked on the first of many trips to Algeria with a team of entomologists. He returned the following year and completed his first two works inspired by the region, Les Terrasses de Laghouat and L'Oued M'sila après l'Orage. During his third trip in 1886, Dinet, along with thirteen other artists including Paul Leroy and Baron Arthur Chassériau, formed the Société des Peintres Orientalistes Français with Jean-Léon Gérôme and Benjamin-Constant as honorary presidents, and Léonce Bénédite, Conservator of the Musée du Luxembourg, as president. | | In 1888, Dinet took important steps to solidify his growing interest in North Africa: he enrolled in formal Arabic classes at the Oriental Language School in Paris and returned to Algeria for a fourth time, accompanied by the young guide, Sliman Ben Ibrahim, with whom Dinet was to eventually live and collaborate with for many years. Dinet's work was displayed in the Algerian pavilion at the Universal Exhibition of 1889, where he would also win the silver medal for painting, and following this surge of publicity, Dinet helped found the Société Nationale des Beaux-Arts along with thirteen other artists. In 1904, after spending many months of each year in Algeria, Dinet decided to create a more permanent base for himself in-country and bought a house in the southern Saharan city of Bou-Saada. | | Delving deeper into Orientalist themes with his work now spanning two continents, Dinet had a respected place among the desert culture from which he drew inspiration. Having rejected early representations of the Maghreb modelled after exotic scenes taken from Greek and Roman antiquity, Dinet was a stunning realist, focused more on the interactions between natives, representations of women and manifestations of the Muslim religion. Despite his numerous paintings of nude Algerian youths – he was, surprisingly, never wanting for indigenous models – Dinet's paintings lack the frank eroticism of his counterparts who illustrated an Orient full of reclining odalisques oozing sensuality. | | Employing the use of photography to capture the fleeting expressions of his models, Dinet's cinematic approach was far removed from the disengaged reserve of fin-de-siècle aesthetics which lent an air of theatricality. His landscapes lack exaggerated romanticism and his depictions of women, a favourite subject, hold no territorial claims over the eastern body seen through western eyes. With his conversion to Islam in 1908 and made formal in 1913, Dinet used his nudes to express a right to represent beauty as created by God, rather than the purely voyeuristic impressions of imagined, private moments. | | With such composites frequenting the canvases of his contemporaries, it is easy to criticize the Orientalist genre of painting Dinet came to define as perpetuating the mythology of an 'empire of the senses' free from the restraints of western civilization and encompassing a timeless zone of primitivism. Yet, this argument is precisely why Dinet is so important to the history and popularity of Orientalist art. With each brush stroke, Dinet penetrated the deeper themes of family, faith and survival unique to the Saharan life he shared with his subjects instead of skimming the surface decor of earlier Orientalist painters passing through the region. | | Never seeking out the exceptional or strange for subject matter, Dinet believed the mission of his art was to describe the souls of his models, express the essence of a people, and to celebrate his own adopted faith of Islam. With those tasks in mind, Dinet also collaborated with his friend, Ben Ibrahim, on translating and illustrating books about Algeria, such as Khadra, Danseurs des Ouled Nails and Tableaux de la vie Arabe, which became quintessential to foreign understanding and perceptions of North Africa. In the words of Léonce Bénédite, Dinet 'became an Arab, a cultured Arab, who clung desperately to the last vestiges of greatness of his race.' | | Shortly after making the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca, Dinet died in his native France in 1929. Today in Bou-Saada, where he was eventually buried, The Nasreddine-Etienne Dinet Museum stands as a testament to Dinet's unique place in the history of Orientalist painters. Though later on in his career to be found behind the times by his peers, Dinet and his true understanding of Saharan life lend his works encapsulating the history and peoples of Algeria an authenticity rarely surpassed. The art critic Camille Mauclair predicted Dinet's staggering importance in the history of Orientalist painters: 'Later on, they (Dinet's canvases) will be incomparable references; they will have fixed without the coldness of archaeology a civilization and a race called upon to transform themselves to the point of travesty by the fatalities of a 'modernism' that is slowly killing the Orient.' By allowing his models to face forward rather than backward to suit the tastes of a time obsessed with antiquity, the work of Etienne Dinet acts as a rich cultural currency towards understanding a way of life now transformed yet far from forgotten.

Braun (see Wellcome Collection 17870i). | | | There are some artists of rare ability, of extreme sincerity, who are astonishing observers, far more conscientious than one can imagine, who spent enormous amounts of time and who lavish superior talent to give us just the emotion which might be produced by photography. M. Dagnan-Bouveret is one of these artists. | Le Siecle 1885. | | In the latter half of the 19th century, French society stood at the crossroads of tradition and modernisation. Nowhere is this tension more evident than in the work of Pascal Dagnan-Bouveret (1852–1929), a realist painter whose oeuvre captures the quiet transformation of rural France. The present work, painted in 1882, is a prime example of how art can reflect and support social progress. La Vaccination became part of a national narrative that celebrated science, health, and the expansion of modern values into rural life. | | Dagnan-Bouveret was a leading figure in Academic Realism, a style characterised by meticulous attention to detail, idealised yet naturalistic figures, and a focus on moral or social themes. Born in Paris, the son of a tailor, he entered the École des Beaux-Arts in 1869; among his tutors were Alexandre Cabanel and Jean-Léon Gérôme. During his studies he formed a close friendship with Gustave Courtois. His education was briefly stalled by the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune; resuming in 1872 when he entered Gérôme's atelier. Dagnan-Bouveret was heavily influenced by both classical techniques and the emerging Naturalist movement. Uniquely, he was also one of the first French artists to integrate photography into his process, allowing for a level of precision and emotional nuance rarely seen in academic works of the time. | | Dagnan-Bouveret married Coutois' cousin Anne-Marie in 1879, the couple spending a great deal of time in Corre, a village in the Franche-Comté region of north-eastern France. The artist's Salon debut came in 1875, and he became a regular exhibitor there, as well as at the Salon de la Société Nationale des Beaux-Arts, the Exposition Universelle -winning major prizes in 1889 and 1900- and the Salon de Champ-de-Mars. He was elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts of the Institut de France in 1900, one of the youngest painters to ever receive this honour. | | La Vaccination portrays a rural family gathered in a modest interior, probably a schoolroom, as a doctor administers a smallpox vaccine to a child. The setting is humble, the figures understated, yet deeply expressive. The mother, seated, gently restrains the child while others look on with solemn curiosity. The doctor, dressed in formal attire, appears calm and deliberate. The overall mood is one of quiet dignity, reflecting both the human vulnerability of the scene and the trust placed in modern medicine. Through its naturalistic lighting, soft colours, and photographic realism, Dagnan-Bouveret elevates what might seem a mundane act into a moment of profound emotional and cultural significance. The painting captures a transitional moment: the encroachment of scientific rationalism into the realm of rural tradition, handled not with drama but with empathy. | | The early history of the work is well recorded; it is listed in the stock books of Goupil & Cie, Paris, for 1882: '16415, Vaccine, 20-12-82, Londres @ H. Turner Esq, Dagnan Bouveret avec portage de Benefice [with profit sharing], 14-4-83'. Founded in 1850 by Auguste Goupil (1806-1893), Goupil & Cie were a central force in the French art market. Dealing in art works by the major academic, realist, romantic and Barbizon painters of the day, and also licencing and distributing reproduction prints, at their zenith, the business had offices in Paris, New York, London (established by Ernest Gambart), Brussels and The Hague. In 1884 the business was succeeded by Boussod, Valadon & Co. and continued until 1919. | | According to Goupil's records, the painting was sold to H. Turner, who is the listed lender when the work was exhibited in 1883. It is likely that Goupil's purchaser was Henry James Turner (1831-1924), a successful industrialist, who assembled a large collection of art by contemporary British and continental artists (Turner was also the owner of On the Roofs by Benjamin-Constant, which is featured in the current sale, see lot 25). Following Turner's purchase of the work, it was exhibited at the Paris Salon in 1883, the Royal Academy in 1884 -the artist's only submission to the famous London exhibition- and the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1889. | | The 1889 Exposition Universelle was one of the most ambitious world's fairs of the 19th century. It celebrated the centenary of the French Revolution and served as a platform to project France's industrial, scientific, and artistic achievements. Among its most iconic symbols was the unveiling of the Eiffel Tower, itself a triumph of modern engineering. With this backdrop, La Vaccination was exhibited in the Palais des Beaux-Arts, part of the fair's Fine Arts Pavilion. Its inclusion speaks to the painting's alignment with the fair's themes: progress, health, and the moral duty of the state to modernise and educate its population. By depicting vaccination - a then-controversial practice in many rural areas - the painting subtly endorsed France's growing public health initiatives and reinforced a sense of national unity through shared scientific progress. | | Dagnan-Bouveret's technique is crucial to the painting's impact. His use of photographic references allowed for subtle facial expressions, delicate skin tones, and lifelike body language. These details lend credibility and intimacy to the scene. The balanced composition—with figures arranged in a semicircle around the doctor—creates a sense of shared focus and emotional weight. His method anticipated modern realism, even as he remained rooted in academic traditions. The inclusion of the work at the 1889 Exposition Universelle cemented Dagnan-Bouveret's reputation as a socially aware artist who could translate complex themes into accessible imagery. But this is more than a depiction of a medical procedure; it is a celebration of science and progress aimed to reassure a nation facing change. Through his technical skill and emotional insight, Dagnan-Bouveret has captured this moment of quiet revolution. | | We are grateful to the late Professor Gabriel P. Weisberg for confirming the authenticity of the present lot on the basis of photographs.

provenance: Anon. sale, Waddington's, Toronto, circa 1980. | Private collection, North America. | | Léon Bazile Perrault was a leading figure of late 19th century French painting, admired for his technique and his sensitive portrayals of childhood and mythological subject matter. Born in Poitiers in 1832, he trained in Paris under François-Édouard Picot and later worked closely with William Adolphe Bouguereau, absorbing the classical discipline and luminous surface finish that characterise the academic tradition. Through them, Perrault also inherited an admiration for the 18th century masters Jean-Antoine Watteau and François Boucher, whose spirit of grace and refinement he carried forward into his own work. | | Perrault began exhibiting at the Paris Salon in 1861 and quickly established a successful career during the Second Empire, a period in which the bourgeois public increasingly developed an interest in art that offered visual pleasure and emotional escape. His compositions, from mythological idylls and allegories to genre scenes and portraits, responded perfectly to this demand. He received several Salon distinctions, including an honourable mention in 1864, a second-class medal in 1876, and in 1887 he was appointed Chevalier de la Légion d'Honneur. | | Although he mastered many academic genres, Perrault is especially celebrated for his images of children, which he portrayed with extraordinary delicacy. These works reflect the 19th century conception of childhood, presenting youth as a state of grace, vulnerability and charm. In the present work, Perrault depicts a moment of mourning, with a mother on a prie-dieu accompanied by her young children. This intimate scene reveals the vulnerability of the sitters and the quiet depth of their despair, while also demonstrating Perrault's ability to unite academic refinement with genuine emotional resonance. | | By the end of his career, he was hors concours at the Salon, exhibiting without jury approval, and his reputation had become firmly established in France and abroad. Perrault died in Royan in 1908. His paintings are today held in several museum collections including Bordeaux, Poitiers, La Rochelle and Stuttgart.

Ross, William Bouguereau: Catalogue Raisonné of his Painted Work, New York, 2010, p. 299, no. 1895/08, illustrated. | | In Fardeau agréable all Bouguereau's formidable prowess is distilled onto the canvas in two engaging young sisters and the pastoral idyll in which they exist; the result is an image of beauty at its purest in the mind of the artist. This is art for art's sake with Bouguereau giving all his attention to the flawless depiction of the figures, spurning any sense of narrative. The composition is dominated by the two sisters in an idealised image of their humble existence. Pastoral subjects such as this, almost always a single peasant girl or two sisters, became the subject matter for some of Bouguereau's most revered and popular works. | | While some French artists of the Realist movement such as Jean-François Millet and Léon Augustin Lhermitte sought to faithfully depict peasant life and its labours, Bouguereau romanticised it and here we see a serene, innocent scene unburdened by any trace of social or economic hardship. In striving to achieve a vision of idyllic rural youth he deliberately ignores the realities of political, industrial and urban life of 19th late century France. According to Alfred Nettement, a student at the Académie Julien, his teacher Bouguereau 'had an absolute horror of what we would call realism and he always said that reality is charming when it borrows a gleam of poetry from the imagination'1. | | The sisters are set before a landscape and sky which not only attest to Bouguereau's skill as a landscape painter but are redolent of late 19th century taste. The first half of the century saw the industrial revolution change pastoral landscapes in Europe and America for ever and as manufacturing increased and urban centres expanded, so did nostalgia for an unspoilt countryside and peasant life. In Fardeau agréable, as in nearly all of Bouguereau's work, the industrial age is not evident, no buildings mar the landscape, and no smoke clouds the skies of the imagined Arcadia. Bouguereau raises his figures above the harsh truth of day-to-day existence in the French peasant countryside and exalts the joy and tenderness of youth and the beauty of nature. | | The younger sister can be identified as Yvonne, one of Bouguereau's favourite models. Little biographical information is known about Yvonne and her two sisters, Jeanne and Marguerite, however they probably lived in La Rochelle as they came regularly to the Bouguereau household and were treated like family. They provided much inspiration for Bouguereau who was born in the area and spent his summers there in the 1890s to escape the social and professional pressures of Paris. The growth of Yvonne and her sisters is recorded in Bouguereau's work of the 1890s, from Yvonne's first appearance in Allant à la Fontaine in 1893 (J. B. Speed Museum, Louisville, Kentucky) at the age of perhaps five or six, we see her grow up as Bouguereau used her as a model until the end of his life. | | Often Bouguereau's figures appear contemplative or distracted, far away in a daydream, however here he seems intent on portraying Yvonne's character as well as her likeness. She gazes engagingly out of the canvas with the confidence and innocence of youth fixing the viewer with an expression full of emotion and intelligence. The elder sister stands on the cusp of womanhood and the dashes of colour Bouguereau has added in the form of wildflowers in the lower left, not only add colour to the composition but come to symbolise the flowering of youth, connotations which would not have been lost on his audience. Bouguereau has been lauded for his mastery of rendering the human figure and nowhere is this more evident than in Fardeau agréable. The sisters sit together in perfect balance and harmony, their movement natural as they pass through the landscape, briefly interrupted by the viewer. | | Great care and consideration are given to every passage and every detail and the execution of the interlocked hands is a perfect example of this meticulous attention. To achieve such authenticity in his figures Bouguereau became a master of the academic style. While working on an oil such as this he would produce many preparatory drawings paying close attention to each individual detail, working and reworking the important parts of the composition ensuring he had full freedom and confidence when setting paint to canvas. Unlike many of his contemporaries, he also preferred to use life models instead of adapting to use photographs as can be seen in fig. 1 which shows Bourguereau in the summer of 1898 working on Les deux soeurs, 1899 and features Yvonne three years after her appearance in Fardeau agréable. | | The latter period of Bouguereau's career from which Fardeau agréable dates followed the great successes of his classical, mythological and religious subjects of his earlier oeuvre and was ushered in by his association with the art dealer Durand-Ruel in the 1860s. To cater to the tastes of his patrons and particularly the international market, Bouguereau shifted his choice of subjects away from the historical and religious and towards the romanticised images of the pastoral, of the type we see here. This resulted in an appetite for Bouguereau's work in North America which neared insatiable in the later years of the 19th century fuelled by first by the French dealer Paul Durand-Ruel and then solidified by Durand-Ruel's foremost competitor, Adolphe Goupil. Between 1866 and 1887, Bouguereau would sell ten to twelve works per year to Goupil for an agreed upon sum, and Goupil then sold approximately nine out of every ten to dealers outside of France, mostly to Wallis in London and Knoedler in New York. In fact, only eight works painted during this period are recorded by Goupil as having been sold to collectors in France. | | The taste of these American patrons would lay the foundation for the collection of many American museums and as art critic and author Clarence Cook noted in his second volume of Art and Artists of Our Time, "Hardly any French painter can be named who is more widely popular in America than Bouguereau. His pictures always meet with a ready sale at large prices, and at the exhibitions they are sure of approval from the majority of the visitors, who would probably pass by Delacroix, Decamps, or Puvis de Chavannes, with small notice, or none at all"2. Fardeau agréable formed part of this tradition when it was acquired by Pittsburgh based financier and iron magnate Alexander McBurney Byers, directly from Knoedler just twenty-four days after it entered the galleries' inventory. | | 1A. Nettement, William Bouguereau, L'Académie Julien, January 1908, p. 3, as quoted in M. S. Walker, William Bouguereau, exh. cat., Montreal, 1984, p. 57. | 2As quoted in Fronia E. Wissman, Bouguereau, San Francisco, 1996, p. 108-9.

provenance: Private European collection. |  | The present lot is accompanied by an expertise certificate from Gianni Caffiero and Ivan Samarine dated February 2026 and is included in their numbered archive of the artist's work. |  | Aivazovsky, renowned worldwide for his marine paintings, was a virtuoso of the stormy sea. The artist possessed an astonishing ability to work rapidly, often completing a painting in a single session. It is this lightness and airiness of his brush that lends his works a special expressiveness and vibrancy. |  | The subject matter, the rendering of colour and light, the dramatic sea, and the small, staffage figures of the men - all this is the master's textbook language. The painting vividly expresses the desire to convey the power of nature, its superiority over the weakness of the small man, completely defenceless against the unbridled elements. |  | The sea on the canvas lives, breathes, and moves. The artist masterfully depicts it in numerous shades of blue, from an almost blackish blue in the depths to a transparent turquoise near the shore. A masterful play of light makes the sea in the background dark and threatening, while the foreground is illuminated by bright reflections, like a ray of hope sent to the shipwrecked survivors. The snow-white foaming crests of the waves are painted with meticulous care; they rise from the surface like two hands reaching out to grasp a person and pull him back into the depths. |  | The painting's composition emphasizes the scale of the confrontation between man and nature. Enormous waves, rising in powerful billows, are ready to engulf everything in their path. Against their backdrop, the tiny figures of the shipwrecked survivors seem like grains of sand in an ocean of raging elements. This is a characteristic technique of Aivazovsky and his school, when depicting the majesty of nature. The log from the wrecked ship in the foreground once again recalls the uncontrollable force of the elements. The anxious, restless rhythm of the waves conveys a sense of confusion and fear before the indomitable force of the sea storm. The artist masterfully utilizes chiaroscuro contrasts. The dark masses of water and sky are offset by bright highlights, creating a unique emotional richness in the work.

After moving to Paris in 1891, his work began to reflect the influence of the Symbolist movement, particularly the Nabis group. His style evolved from Impressionist tendencies towards a Pre-Raphaelite approach, and like many artists of his generation, he later travelled to Florence to study the Old Masters, adopting techniques such as tempera painting. Each of these artistic encounters left a lasting imprint on his work. | | Robinson's academic training is evident in the precision of his line and form. He often depicted solitary figures most often women or children set in rural or pastoral landscapes. His use of harmonious, muted colour schemes lent these allegorical themes a sense of calm rather than dramatic intensity. The Little Shepherdess embodies these qualities, with its lone figure in a tranquil pastoral setting, rendered in a subdued palette that enhances its quiet, contemplative mood.

provenance: The sitter and thence by descent. | Sale, Christie's, London, 19 November 2004, lot 148. | Private collection, UK (acquired at the above sale). | | Literature | D. McKibbin, Sargent's Boston, Boston, 1956, pp. 92 and 97. | | This portrait is a study for one of the figures in Sargent's 1920-22 oil Some General Officers of the Great War (National Portrait Gallery, London). | | Sir Charles Macpherson Dobell (1869-1954) was born in Quebec and after his primary education in Canada, attended Charterhouse in England for two years as his father had emigrated to Liverpool due to his employment in the lumber trade. He returned to Canada for his preliminary military training before being commissioned into the 1st Bn. Royal Welsh Fusiliers in August 1890. He served his military apprenticeship in Britain's colonial wars, staying with the 1st Bn. for the next five years, learning how to command men. Postings with the 2nd Bn. The Royal Welsh Fusiliers in Crete, South Africa and China (suppressing the Boxer Rebellion) followed. | | Dobell's rise in the Edwardian decade was meteoric, reflecting his talent as an officer but also his ambition and connections. He left Staff College in 1904 for command in Nigeria, followed by periods in England and South Africa. During this time he married, in March 1908, a widow with two children who duly had their own daughter in South Africa in 1912. On the eve of the outbreak of the First World War he was Inspector-General of the West African Frontier Force. | | The declaration of war found Dobell on leave in England, but given his African experience he was soon given command of the British troops and eventually the Allied Forces in the two German colonies of Togoland and Cameroon. The German defence in Cameroon was stiff and the fighting attritional, but the Allied forces prevailed in February 1916. The victory was celebrated given how stagnant the campaign in France and Flanders had become and Dobell's star rose further. | | Dobell was next posted to the Middle-East in June 1916. His involvement in two failed attempts to take Gaza in 1917 are seen as perhaps the only blot on an otherwise pristine record. Although Gaza was eventually taken by the subsequent command, thanks somewhat to the preparations laid by Dobell and his superiors, he could not escape judgement for the two bloody, failed attempts at the objective from London which was hungry for news of success. On his return home he was immediately posted to India where he would stay until 1920. | | Through his career Dobell was mentioned in despatches nine times, he retired with the honorary rank of lieutenant-general in 1923 and retained links with the Regiment up to the months preceding his death in 1954.

provenance: With Frost and Reed, London. | With Richard Green, London. | Anon. sale, Sotheby's, London, 7 May 2009, lot 39. | With Richard Green, London. | Property of a Gentleman (acquired from the above in 2009). | | Exhibited | London, Richard Green Fine Paintings, Sir Alfred Munnings KVCO, PRA, An Artist's Life, 14 November - 14 December 2012, no. 49. | | Literature | Exh. cat, Sir Alfred Munnings KVCO, PRA, An Artist's Life, Richard Green Fine Paintings London, 2012, no. 49, illustrated. | | Munnings had a childhood fascination with carriage horses. Growing up at his family's mill in Suffolk, he watched and often drew the multitudes of dray horses as they waited for their wagonloads of grain to be unloaded. His first competent drawing of a harnessed horse was done at around age six of a toy horse he had named Merrylegs .1 | | Additionally, Munnings recalls in his memoirs 'A distinct scene from my earliest days, which for some strange reason remains clear and more unclouded than others, is my Aunt Rosa's wedding, with grey horses and white rosettes. I see them trotting up to Walsham Hall, the old farmhouse where my grandmother lived...They were no doubt quite ordinary greys, but let me cling to my dream of beauty' 2 | | The present work has traditionally been associated directly with Their Majestie's return from Ascot, (Tate Britian, NO4956). On further research, however, it appears that the work is in fact earlier and an important forerunner to the Tate work, not a direct preparatory sketch. The work belongs to series of paintings executed between 1909-1911 depicting carriage horses.3 | | The solid red livery and the horses' docked tails give evidence that the figures are not from the Royal Household but rather privately owned. Queen Victoria set a precedent for banning the docking of horses' tails in the Royal stables. Although the setting for this work as in the others from the series is unidentified, Munnings always painted from direct observation, so all the details are factual. The postilion or rider stands on the near or left side of two horses from which each pair is controlled and guided by a mounted rider rather than being driven by a coachman from the 'box' (seat) on the carriage. The paintings in this series are without doubt forerunners to his paintings of the Royal Family going to and from Ascot near Windsor painted in 1925. | | What is unusual in this sketch is the clarity with which Munnings painted the face of the postilion. This precision and the stillness of the postilion are juxtaposed with the summary detail of the two horses. They were obviously restless, standing still which is suggested by the perceived movement of the hind legs. This agitation is also evidenced by the tight hold the postilion has on the reins and that the horses are standing firm in their leather traces. If the horses had been relaxed the leather would have been slack. | | Time spent sketching horses prior to working on a larger scale in oil was highly important part of Munnings' process. Spending hours in the company of the horses, painting in both oil and watercolour gave Munnings an intimate knowledge not only of each individual horse's anatomy and appearance, but also their character. This process, combined with a life spent around horses and a deep understanding of their nature translates to the vitality and authenticity with which Munnings depicts the equine form, as seen in the present work and across his oeuvre. | | We are grateful to Lorian Peralta-Ramos for her assistance in cataloguing this lot. | | 1Munnings, An Artist's Life, vol. Further influences came from travels to Paris and Venice in 1883, where his exposure to continental art broadened his palette. By 1885, Fortescue had moved from the industrial Midlands to the Cornish coast at Newlyn. |  | His career developed steadily. He exhibited regularly at the Royal Academy and was actively involved in local artistic life. Fortescue frequently returned to working subjects such as fishermen, blacksmiths, and churchgoers, all while capturing the everyday of those living and working around him. |  | The present lot shows the interior of the church of St Pol de Léon (commonly known as Paul Parish church), in the village of Paul, above Mousehole in Cornwall. The church architecture is a dominant feature, yet the stone, plaster, and brass of the interior frame the worshippers rather than distract from them. provenance: Given by the artist to the sitter's mother. | By descent to the sitter. | | This work is listed in the Laura Knight catalogue raisonné being prepared by John Croft under no. 0634. | | In 1939 at the outbreak of war Laura and Harold Knight left their residence at Langford Place in London, the staff having already abandoned the house at the announcement of the outbreak. Harold travelled to Scotland to complete a portrait commission, which had not been cancelled because of the war, before joining Laura in the Malvern Hills, already a favourite pre-war retreat for the couple. | | They stayed at The British Camp hotel, Wynds Point (now The Malvern Hills Hotel) and Laura found herself hunting interesting subjects to paint. She later wrote, 'I stayed in Malvern, where to keep myself from going crackers, I painted the nearest thing to hand: the old back garden gate belonging to the hotel, and almost the last rose of summer, anything... no matter what... so long as I didn't stop to think.' (Laura Knight, The Magic of Line, 1965, p. 273). Not until mid-1940 however, was her interest piqued by the arrival at the hotel of a young family from Italy whose portraits she eagerly proceeded to paint. | | As war raged in France and with Italy on the brink of entering on the side of Nazi Germany, Italian families began considering evacuation. The sitter of this portrait recalls the time as follows: | | 'Shortly before this portrait was painted in May 1940, my Mother, Sister and I had a hazardous escape from our home in Italy just before the battle of Dunkirk. | | My Mother had been advised that Malvern's remoteness would be ideal to escape the risks of bombardment – a mistaken assessment, as it happened. Evidently, the German bombers, if they failed to unload all their bombs on Birmingham or Coventry, would wheel round and drop them over the Malvern Hills. | | We were staying in the British Camp Hotel in Malvern and it is there that we encountered Laura Knight who then asked my mother if she could paint me. | | As a seven year old boy, and given the circumstances, I was preoccupied with aeroplanes and maps. The portrait indicates the acute anxiety I remember feeling at the time particularly having recently had to escape from another country.' | | The anxiety he felt was not misplaced. Laura Knight describes how at the hotel 'one evening, a bomb explosion close by nearly shook us all out of our seats at the dining tables. This had been dropped less than half a mile away on the western side of the hills' (Ibid, Knight, p. 274). | | The tenderness with which she painted this portrait succeeds in capturing the unique anxiety and preoccupation of a child displaced by war, but also a young boy's curious fascination for the aeroplanes he could see and hear overhead. Only a few years later she would be painting the men who were sending the planes and from whom he was fleeing. | | At the end of the war Knight was invited to travel to Europe and cover the Nuremberg Trials as part of her commission as an official war artist. From the Malvern Hills painting hop-pickers and evacuees, she now found herself in the Nuremberg courtroom face to face with the main perpetrators of the war. She later recalled a chilling moment in the courtroom; 'Goering glanced up at me today. He looks a terribly sick man. For the first time he wears a red scarf round his neck and a travelling rug round his knees – he has a bad cold, by the look of his nose (Ibid, Knight, p. 289). | | This cold description and the muted tones of the masterwork which followed are in stark contrast to the warmth, vitality and emotion with which Knight painted the Malvern hotel portrait. The painting provides a snapshot of a unique period of time and of a boy for whom she was clearly quite taken.
